text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, recuperating from double pneumonia, worked on official papers for most of the day on Tuesday and went for his first walk outdoors in two weeks, chief Kremlin doctor Sergei Mironov said.
"He's in a completely satisfactory condition," Mironov said in an interview with Reuters shortly after seeing Yeltsin at the president's Gorky-9 country residence outside Moscow.
"He worked on documents for more than seven hours. It's fairly stressful work, government documents. He's not only signing them but correcting them."
Mironov felt that Yeltsin, 65, was overdoing things at that pace and suggested that for now he should keep to about four hours of work a day.

"For the first time he went outside and went for a walk at his country residence. He went around the house...When we arrived he was talking to his youngest grandson. It was a lively conversation," he said.

Mironov said Yeltsin, who moved on Monday evening to the country residence after 12 days in hospital, was still being treated but might be able to attend a summit in Moscow next week and then travel abroad.
"Double pneumonia requires a rather long treatment with medicines," he said. "But now on the whole the medicines are aimed at strengthening the body...It's a matter of time."

Mironov said Yeltsin was "morally worn down" by going back into hospital just two weeks after returning to the Kremlin following a six-month break during which he had open heart surgery on November 5.
"He was feeling uncomfortable and morally uncomfortable with his voters," Mironov said. "But illness is illness."

He now was "convalescing physically and morally" but Mironov cautioned that he would be prone to fatigue for a time and had to take life easy: "If we had pneumonia, we would have the same syndrome, feeling tired and down and rather quick to tire.
"This of course will last for a rather long time. If you force things, it cannot lead to good, rapid results. We must just find an adequate threshold," he added.
Mironov said doctors were trying to limit Yeltsin's contact with outsiders to reduce the risk of new infections and to help him sleep longer and in a more regular pattern.
He said Yeltsin sat down to work at his desk at 6 a.m. on Tuesday and worked until 1.30 p.m. After lunch, he watched television and read newspapers before working some more.

Asked when Yeltsin would be able to return to the Kremlin, Mironov said: "I would not like to fix an exact date. But nonetheless the work schedule which the president had before this illness being remains on his agenda for the time being."
Yeltsin is due to attend a summit of leaders of former Soviet states in Moscow on January 29 and then receive French President Jacques Chirac on February 2.
Mironov said Yeltsin planned to fly to The Hague on February 3 for talks the following day with Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, current holder of the European Union presidency.
Mironov said Yeltsin had been working on his annual state of the nation address to parliament, a 70-page document due to be presented on February 11.
Asked about pressure on Yeltsin from opponents who want him to step down on health grounds, Mironov said doctors saw no medical reasons to suggest he could not continue running Russia.
"There are no medical indications, as of today, that suggest that Boris Nikolayevich will not be able to work as president of our country," Mironov told U.S. cable network MSNBC earlier on Tuesday.

"Of course, his recent heart operation and the double pneumonia he now has do not create, as of today, the most favourable working mood, but nonetheless Boris Nikolayevich is looking to the future with great optimism and would consider that...he can continue his state duties," he added.
